explanation: Spider fossils go back at least 300 million years, long before the earliest dinosaurs. Their relatives the scorpions are older still, with fossils over 400 million years old.

claims.text: The oldest known fossils of true spiders are at least 300 million years old.
The earliest dinosaurs appeared about 230 to 240 million years ago.
Scorpion fossils more than 400 million years old are known.

writerNotes: Self-check (guide 9.3), all eleven codes confirmed true. The selfCheck field itself is left out because the CNT-1 item schema refuses it as an unknown key, so the codes are recorded here. lint: content:check reports no errors and no warnings for this item. claims: three listed; high: c1 (date), c2 (date) and c3 (date). datasets: no pinned dataset in content/datasets/manifest.json covers animal or plant biology (it holds countries, languages, currencies, cities, elements, Nobel Prizes, Olympic Games, World Cups, art collections and Natural Earth), so none applies, and the high-risk claims need web evidence from checker A; one search on the oldest spider fossils should cover c1; c2 is widely documented and c3 can share a search with c1. rivalTest: Argued for dinosaurs, the textbook image of 'ancient', against small modern-looking spiders. Both values are conservative: spider fossils of about 310 million years are widely reported, and older spider-like arachnids exist, so the gap of at least 60 million years holds under any dating on offer. counterintuitive is false because many players already think of spiders as ancient. volatility: evergreen, a settled fact that cannot change; no time words, and nothing rests on knowledge newer than mid-2026. regional: both groups are known everywhere. style: Oxford spelling, plain hyphens only, explanation of 28 words. myths: screened against content/reference/myths.json; no entry matches. mystery and encore: nothing of either kind in a comparison item. doubts: c1 says 'true spiders' because older spider-like arachnids such as Attercopus are not true spiders; the item's answer holds either way.
